# `nish/net/tls/record-server`

A TLS 1.3 server over a byte stream: the record layer of `nish/net/tls/record` wrapped around `nish/net/tls`'s `TlsServer`, sans-IO. Bytes the client sent go in, bytes to send come out, and once the handshake is done application data flows both ways.

```ts
import {
  TLS_RECORD_AGAIN,
  TLS_RECORD_DATA,
  TLS_RECORD_DONE,
  TLS_RECORD_IDLE_LIMIT,
  TLS_RECORD_INVALID,
  TLS_RECORD_MAX_KEY_UPDATES,
  TLS_RECORD_PIPE,
  TLS_RECORD_RESET,
  TLS_RECORD_SIGN,
  TLS_RECORD_STATE_CLOSED,
  TLS_RECORD_STATE_FAILED,
  TLS_RECORD_STATE_HANDSHAKE,
  TLS_RECORD_STATE_OPEN,
  TLS_RECORD_TICKET,
  TLS_RECORD_WANT_READ,
  TLS_RECORD_WANT_WRITE,
  TlsRecordPools,
  TlsRecordServer,
} from "nish/net/tls/record-server";
```

```ts
const conn = new TlsRecordServer(new TlsServer(config, random, key));
conn.receive(bytes, 0, n);                 // what the socket read
if ((conn.interest() & TLS_RECORD_SIGN) !== 0) {
  conn.sign(tlsSignEcdsaP256(leaf, conn.signatureInput()));
}
// send conn.output[conn.outputStart .. conn.outputEnd), then conn.consume(sent)
const got: i32 = conn.read(buf, 0, buf.length);   // application data
```

<scalar-card title="TlsRecordPools" icon="phosphor/regular/cube" href="#tlsrecordpools">

The four pools a connection's record buffers are borrowed from: `output` and `plain` for `TlsRecordServer`'s fields of those names, `scratch` for the buffer it opens a record's content into, and `reader` for its record reader's buffer.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="TlsRecordServer" icon="phosphor/regular/cube" href="#tlsrecordserver">

One TLS 1.3 server connection over a stream.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>

<scalar-detail title="What it adds to `TlsServer`">

Records around the handshake messages:
ServerHello (or HelloRetryRequest) in the clear, the rest of the server's
flight — EncryptedExtensions through Finished — in as few records as fit
under the handshake keys once it is signed, which is one record for RFC
8448 §3's trace, and every key installed at the record boundary RFC 8446
§5.1 puts it on. The middlebox-compatibility `change_cipher_spec` of §D.4:
the server sends one right after its first handshake message when the
client sent a session id, and drops the client's from its first ClientHello
until its Finished. Alerts (§6) both ways: `close_notify` ends the client's
stream, `user_canceled` is passed over, any other alert ends the
connection, and a refusal of this module's or of `TlsServer`'s is sent as a
fatal alert under whatever keys the server writes with. KeyUpdate (§4.6.3)
both ways: the client's moves the read keys on and, when it asks, the
server answers with its own; `keyUpdate` sends one, and the writer sends
one by itself before a key has protected `TLS_KEY_UPDATE_RECORDS` records.
More than `TLS_RECORD_IDLE_LIMIT` records in a row that carry nothing for
the caller — KeyUpdates among them, which each cost two key derivations —
are refused. A stream that ends without `close_notify` is truncation, but
only once the records still waiting for the caller have been read.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Borrowed buffers">

The record being read, the record being opened, the
bytes to send and the application data waiting for the caller each live in
an array borrowed from a `TlsRecordPools` when the connection first needs
it, kept while the connection lasts, and given back zeroed with
`BufferPool.giveSecret` when it ends (`start`, `wipe`, `release`), so a
slot with no connection holds none of them, a connection that has finished
its handshake allocates nothing that outlives a record, and a slot can be
handed the next connection with `start`. Each give-back zeroes the whole
buffer, so it happens once a connection rather than once a record. The handshake's messages are
sealed straight out of `TlsServer`'s own buffers, and the application
secrets are copied into this slot's fields, so a slot that hands its
`TlsServer` the next connection with `restart` runs every handshake after
the first without moving the arena, whichever suite it negotiates; a
KeyUpdate's key install leaves nothing either (TLS-3 in
`docs/security/tls.md`). When the caller leaves application data unread
for long enough to fill its buffer, records stay in the reader and
`interest` stops asking for reads, which is how the peer is made to wait.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Secrets">

Each traffic secret is a `Secret<u8[]>` (`nish:secret`):
`TlsServer` holds the handshake's in its `TlsSecretPool`s, and this slot
holds the two application traffic secrets in four readonly fields, one per
direction and hash length, with `readHash` and `writeHash` saying which of
each pair is live (0 when neither is). A secret is copied out of
`TlsServer` as it is installed and the server's copy is zeroed, as are the
handshake secret once the flight is signed and the ephemeral key once the
ServerHello is written, or the handshake fails; a KeyUpdate overwrites the
live field in place with the next secret. Every way the connection ends
wipes what it holds: a failure of any kind (`fail`, the client's error
alert, a truncated stream, `abort`) wipes both directions' keys, both
secrets and everything `TlsServer` still holds once the last alert is
sealed; the server's `close_notify`, once sealed, wipes the write
direction, the client's the read direction, and `close` the resumption
master secret; and `wipe` (which `wipeKeys` calls when the carrier closes
the slot) and `start` wipe the rest. No secret leaves either object but
through `expose`, so a secret cannot be logged or kept outside
this module and `nish/net/tls` (TLS-1 in `docs/security/tls.md`).

</scalar-detail>

Refusals are alerts, never panics. Written from RFC 8446 §4.6.3, §5, §6
and §D.4, not ported from another implementation.

## TlsRecordPools

The four pools a connection's record buffers are borrowed from: `output`
and `plain` for `TlsRecordServer`'s fields of those names, `scratch` for the
buffer it opens a record's content into, and `reader` for its record
reader's buffer. A carrier with many slots makes one set
with a ceiling of its slot count and points every slot at it with
`TlsRecordServer.borrowFrom`, so a full server holds what preallocating
every slot would have held and an idle one holds only what earlier
connections left on the free lists. Each buffer goes back zeroed
(`BufferPool.giveSecret`): it held plaintext, or handshake bytes.

```ts
class TlsRecordPools
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new TlsRecordPools(ceiling: i32)` | Four empty pools of `ceiling` buffers each; nothing is made until a slot needs it. |
| `output: BufferPool` | Lends each slot its `output` buffer, where sealed records wait to be sent. |
| `plain: BufferPool` | Lends each slot its `plain` buffer, where opened application data waits to be read. |
| `reader: BufferPool` | Lends each slot its record reader's buffer. |
| `scratch: BufferPool` | Lends each slot the buffer a record's content is opened into. |
| `lent(): i32` | How many buffers of the four pools are lent now: 0 once every connection has given its back. |
| `made(): i32` | How many buffers the four pools have made: their high-water mark together. |

## TlsRecordServer

One TLS 1.3 server connection over a stream. Allocate one per slot, hand it
each connection's `TlsServer` with `start`, and drive it with `receive`,
`consume`, `read`, `write` and `sign` as `interest` says.

The fields are readable: `state`, `alert` (the alert this server sent, or
0), `peerAlert` (the error alert the client sent, or -1), `peerClosed`
(the client's `close_notify` arrived), `tls` (the handshake: suite, ALPN,
server name, exporter secret), and the two protections with their
sequence numbers. `padding` is how many zero bytes each protected record
the server writes carries after its content type (§5.4), 0 unless the
caller sets it.

```ts
class TlsRecordServer
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new TlsRecordServer(tls: TlsServer)` | Makes a slot for `tls` with a pool set of its own, one buffer of each kind, and starts the connection as `start` does. A carrier that shares its pools calls `borrowFrom` right after. |
| `alert: i32` | The alert this server sent, or 0. |
| `closeDue: boolean` | The server has closed and its `close_notify` waits for room in `output`. |
| `keyUpdates: i32` | KeyUpdates taken from the client, against `TLS_RECORD_MAX_KEY_UPDATES`. |
| `output: u8[]` | Bytes to send are `output[outputStart .. outputEnd)`; `empty` until a record is sealed. |
| `outputEnd: i32` | Where the bytes still to send end in `output`. |
| `outputStart: i32` | Where the bytes still to send begin in `output`. |
| `padding: i32` | How many zero bytes each protected record the server writes carries after its content type (§5.4); 0 unless the caller sets it. |
| `peerAlert: i32` | The error alert the client sent, or -1 when it sent none. |
| `peerClosed: boolean` | True once the client's `close_notify` has arrived. |
| `plain: u8[]` | Application data the caller has not read is `plain[plainStart .. plainEnd)`; `empty` until a record brings some. |
| `plainEnd: i32` | Where the application data not yet read ends in `plain`. |
| `plainStart: i32` | Where the application data not yet read begins in `plain`. |
| `readHash: i32` | The hash length of the client's traffic secret in bytes (32 or 48), or 0 before it is known. |
| `readProtection: TlsRecordProtection` | Opens the client's records; its sequence number counts the records read at the current keys. |
| `readonly readTraffic256: Secret<u8[]>` | The client's and the server's current application traffic secrets, for KeyUpdate, each held at both hash lengths: `readHash` and `writeHash` say which of a pair holds the secret, and are 0 before it is known. |
| `readonly readTraffic384: Secret<u8[]>` | The client's current application traffic secret when the hash is SHA-384, 48 bytes. |
| `state: i32` | Where the connection stands: one of the `TLS_RECORD_STATE_*` constants. |
| `tls: TlsServer` | The handshake underneath: read it for the suite, ALPN, server name and exporter secret. |
| `writeHash: i32` | The hash length of the server's traffic secret in bytes (32 or 48), or 0 before it is known. |
| `writeLevel: i32` | The `TLS_LEVEL_*` the server's records are written at. |
| `writeProtection: TlsRecordProtection` | Seals the server's records; its sequence number counts the records written at the current keys. |
| `readonly writeTraffic256: Secret<u8[]>` | The server's current application traffic secret when the hash is SHA-256, 32 bytes. |
| `readonly writeTraffic384: Secret<u8[]>` | The server's current application traffic secret when the hash is SHA-384, 48 bytes. |
| `abort(): void` | The socket failed under the connection: it ends with nothing more sent, and every key it holds wiped. |
| `borrowFrom(pools: TlsRecordPools): void` | Borrows the record buffers from `pools` from now on, a carrier's set its slots share. Whatever is held from the old pools is given back first, zeroed, and dropped with it, so call it on a slot with nothing in flight: the carrier does, right after the constructor. |
| `close(): void` | Closes the server's side (§6.1): a `close_notify`, after which `write` answers `TLS_RECORD_PIPE` and nothing more is sent. What was still owed of the handshake is dropped; application data already written stays ahead of the alert, which waits for room in `output` when there is none. The resumption master secret is wiped, since nothing issues a ticket from it, and the write keys once the `close_notify` is sealed (`sealClose`). Nothing happens once the connection has failed or closed. |
| `consume(n: i32): void` | Lets the first `n` bytes of `output` go, once the socket has taken them, and seals what was waiting for the room. |
| `end(): void` | The client's TCP stream ended. After its `close_notify` that is the orderly end; before it, the stream was cut short — truncation, which an attacker on the path can cause — and the connection fails with nothing sent, since there is nobody left to read it. |
| `fail(alert: i32): void` | Fails the connection with `alert`, sent as a fatal alert under whatever the server writes with now, in the clear before its first keys. What was still owed is dropped: the alert is the last thing the server sends, so once it is sealed every key the connection holds is wiped, the traffic keys and secrets as well as what `TlsServer` holds. |
| `interest(): i32` | What the connection wants next, as `TLS_RECORD_*` bits: read the socket (there is room, and the stream has not ended), write it (`output` holds bytes), `read` (application data, or the end of the client's stream), sign, handle a ticket, or nothing more ever (`TLS_RECORD_DONE`: failed or closed, and everything is sent). |
| `issue(key: Secret<u8[]>, info: TlsTicketKeyInfo, now: i64): boolean` | While `interest` says `TLS_RECORD_TICKET` on an open connection: seals a ticket under `key` (`TlsServer.issue`) and queues its NewSessionTicket. Whether one was queued; either way the resumption master secret is wiped, and no second ticket is issued. |
| `keyUpdate(requestPeer: boolean): i32` | Sends a KeyUpdate now, asking the client to update too when `requestPeer` (§4.6.3). Answers 0, `TLS_RECORD_AGAIN` while the handshake is under way or `output` is full, `TLS_RECORD_PIPE` once the server has closed or the connection failed, or `TLS_RECORD_RESET` when the next keys do not install and the connection fails on it. |
| `read(buf: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | Application data from the client, into `buf[off .. off + len)`: the count, as a socket read answers; 0 at the end of its stream (its `close_notify`) or for a `len` of 0; `TLS_RECORD_AGAIN` when nothing is waiting; `TLS_RECORD_RESET` once the connection has failed; and `TLS_RECORD_INVALID` for a window outside `buf`. Reading makes room, so records the buffer was full for are handled before it answers. |
| `receive(data: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | Takes bytes of the client's stream, `data[off .. off + len)`, and handles every record they complete. Answers how many it took, which is fewer than `len` only when its buffers are full (read `interest` before reading the socket again), or `TLS_RECORD_INVALID` for a window outside `data`. Once the connection has failed, or the client has sent `close_notify`, bytes are taken and dropped (§6.1). |
| `release(): void` | Gives back every record buffer this slot holds, zeroed, and drops what was in them: unsent output, unread application data and a partial record. The carrier calls it when it closes the slot, after the last flush and `wipeKeys`, so a free slot holds no buffer of the pools'. |
| `resume(current: Secret<u8[]>, currentInfo: TlsTicketKeyInfo, previous: Secret<u8[]>, previousInfo: TlsTicketKeyInfo, strikes: TlsTicketStrikes, now: i64): i32` | While `interest` says `TLS_RECORD_TICKET` in the handshake: reads the ClientHello's tickets under the keys the carrier lends (`TlsServer.resume`) and seals the flight that answers it, resumed or in full. Answers 0, or the alert the connection failed with — `internal_error` when no ticket waits. |
| `sealRecord(type: i32, data: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): boolean` | Seals one record of `type` from `data[off .. off + len)` onto `output` under the write protection, padded when it is protected. False, writing nothing, when it does not fit; a refusal from `seal` itself, which only a mistake here could cause, fails the connection. |
| `sign(signature: u8[]): i32` | Takes the signature over `signatureInput()` (DER for ECDSA, as `tlsSignEcdsaP256` answers it) and seals the rest of the flight. Answers 0, or the alert the connection failed with — `internal_error` when no signature is due. |
| `signatureInput(): u8[] \| null` | What the CertificateVerify signs, while `interest` says `TLS_RECORD_SIGN`; `null` otherwise. |
| `space(): i32` | How many bytes `receive` would take now: what the socket should read at most. |
| `start(tls: TlsServer): void` | Starts a new connection in this slot with `tls`, which should be fresh or just restarted (`TlsServer.restart`, which reuses its buffers): every buffer is emptied and given back, zeroed, and the keys of the last connection are wiped; nothing is allocated. A `tls` that has already failed — a configuration or randomness `TlsServer` refused — fails this connection at once, with its alert queued in the clear. |
| `wipe(): void` | Wipes everything this slot holds, which is what `wipeKeys` does: both traffic secrets at both hash lengths, both directions' keys, and everything `TlsServer` holds. The record buffers that hold nothing still needed go back too; a failure's alert waiting in `output` stays until it is sent or `release` drops it. |
| `wipeKeys(): void` | Wipes every key this connection holds: the two application traffic secrets it keeps for KeyUpdate, both directions' keys, and what is left in `TlsServer` (`TlsServer.wipe`). The carrier calls it when a slot is closed, so a free slot holds no key. |
| `write(data: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | Application data for the client, `data[off .. off + len)`: seals as much as fits, in records of at most 2^14 bytes, and answers how much that was, as a socket write does. A KeyUpdate goes first when the key has protected `recordLimit` records, or the client asked for one. `TLS_RECORD_AGAIN` while the handshake is under way or nothing fits, `TLS_RECORD_PIPE` once the server has closed or the connection failed, and `TLS_RECORD_INVALID` for a window outside `data`. |

## Limits

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="16" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_IDLE_LIMIT: i32`

How many records in a row may carry nothing for the caller — a
`change_cipher_spec`, empty application data, a `user_canceled` warning, a
KeyUpdate or a piece of one — before the connection is refused with
`unexpected_message`. Each costs the server work, a KeyUpdate two key
derivations, and none moves the connection on. Sixteen is Go's
`maxUselessRecords`; a record of application data, or of the handshake,
starts the count again.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="64" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_MAX_KEY_UPDATES: i32`

How many KeyUpdates one connection takes from its client before refusing
the next with `unexpected_message`. Each costs one key install, two when
the server answers, which leave nothing in the arena; the cap bounds the
work a client can ask for, as `TLS_RECORD_IDLE_LIMIT` does in a row. A
client that
updates when RFC 8446 §5.5 asks, once per 2^24 records, reaches it after
2^30 records; §4.6.3 itself sets no limit, so one that updates on a clock of
its own is cut off at the sixty-fifth, a trade-off TLS-3 records.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>

## Constants

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="-11" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_AGAIN: i32`

What `read`, `write` and `keyUpdate` answer when they have to wait: Linux's EAGAIN, as `nish:net` spells it.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_DATA: i32`

`read` has application data, or the end of the client's stream, to give.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="16" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_DONE: i32`

Nothing more will happen: the connection failed or closed, and everything to send is sent.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-22" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_INVALID: i32`

What `read` and `write` answer for a window outside the caller's array: Linux's EINVAL.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-32" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_PIPE: i32`

What `write` answers once the server has closed: Linux's EPIPE, as `nish:net` spells it.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-104" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_RESET: i32`

What `read` and `write` answer once the connection has failed: Linux's ECONNRESET, as `nish:net` spells it.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_SIGN: i32`

The server is waiting for its CertificateVerify signature: `signatureInput`, then `sign`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_STATE_CLOSED: i32`

The server's `close_notify` is written; it sends nothing more, and may still read.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_STATE_FAILED: i32`

The connection ended on an alert, sent (`alert`) or received (`peerAlert`), or on a stream cut short.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_STATE_HANDSHAKE: i32`

The handshake is under way.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_STATE_OPEN: i32`

The client's Finished verified: application data flows both ways.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="32" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_TICKET: i32`

A ticket is the carrier's to handle, with the keys and strike register it
lends: during the handshake the ClientHello offers one, so `resume` reads
it; once the connection is open the client may be issued one, so `issue`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_WANT_READ: i32`

There is room for more of the stream: read the socket.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`TLS_RECORD_WANT_WRITE: i32`

`output` holds bytes to send: write the socket.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>
